paragraphs.heading: Disks with arms
paragraphs.text: Spiral galaxies are a class that Edwin Hubble described in his 1936 work The Realm of the Nebulae, which makes them part of the Hubble sequence. Most have a flat, spinning disk of stars, gas and dust around a central crowd of stars called the bulge. Around these there is often a much fainter halo of stars, many of them in globular clusters. The galaxies take their name from the spiral patterns that reach from the center out into the disk.

paragraphs.heading: The spiral arms
paragraphs.text: The spiral arms are long, thin regions of stars curving out from the center. They are where new stars keep forming, and they shine brighter than the rest of the disk because of the young, hot stars living in them. Those stars are blue, and there are many of them. Arm shapes differ by class: Sc and SBc galaxies have loose arms, while Sa and SBa galaxies have tightly wrapped ones.

paragraphs.heading: The central bulge
paragraphs.text: The bulge is a large, tightly packed group of stars at the center. In Sa and SBa galaxies it tends to be large and is usually made of Population II stars, which are old, red and low in metals. In Sc and SBc galaxies the bulge is much smaller and made of young, blue Population I stars. Many bulges are thought to hold a supermassive black hole at their centers; in our own galaxy that black hole is called Sagittarius A*.

paragraphs.heading: Bars
paragraphs.text: Roughly two-thirds of spirals have a bar-shaped band of stars running out from the bulge, and the spiral arms begin at its ends. A bar can be strong or weak. Bars have likely become more common: about 8 billion years ago only around 10% had them, roughly a quarter did 2.5 billion years ago, and today over two-thirds do. The Milky Way is a barred spiral, though the bar is hard to see from Earth's position inside the disk. The best evidence for it comes from several surveys, including one with the Spitzer Space Telescope.

paragraphs.heading: The halo
paragraphs.text: Not every star sits in the disk or bulge; some live in a round halo. The halo seems free of dust, and its stars are much older and lower in metals than those of the disk. Some halo stars come from small galaxies that fall in: the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy is merging with the Milky Way, and some stars in our halo were taken from it. Halo stars sometimes pass through the disk, and a few small red dwarfs near the Sun, such as Kapteyn's Star, are thought to belong to the halo.

paragraphs.heading: Where and how far back
paragraphs.text: Spirals and irregulars together make up about 60% of the galaxies in today's universe. Spirals tend to live in regions where galaxies are sparse, and are seldom found in the centers of galaxy clusters. They also go back a long way. As of 2024 the oldest and most distant known spiral is BRI 1335-0417, whose light took 12.4 billion years to reach Earth.
